description: We are four university students from Türkiye behind FireWatch TR, a free wildfire tracking app already using NASA FIRMS MODIS/VIIRS hotspot data. For this challenge we want to extend our clustering and verification pipeline into a harmonized, cross-sensor burning activity calendar. Skills: Flutter, Node.js/TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Earth observation data, GIS, UI/UX, data visualization, science communication.
summary: When does your region burn? For 25 years, two NASA instruments have answered differently: MODIS and VIIRS use different pixel sizes, different confidence scales, and count the same fire twice. The Fire Almanac of Türkiye makes them speak one language. Our open pipeline merges 988,698 FIRMS detections (2001-2025) into 448,364 real fire events, each with a Trust Score that grows when both satellites agree - and turns them into an interactive calendar anyone can read: pick a province, see its fire weeks, spot the unusual ones. The July 2021 Manavgat-Marmaris disaster stands out at 35x the long-term average, automatically. Fire managers see which weeks need crews in place; communities learn their fire season; researchers download 25 years of cross-calibrated data in one click. We are the team behind FireWatch TR, a live wildfire app on Google Play - this almanac is the memory our live alerts were missing.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. The Fire Almanac answers one question: when does a region burn? A weekly calendar (2001-2025) shows burning activity for all of Türkiye or any province, with unusual weeks flagged by their deviation from the long-term mean. A map shows each harmonized fire event with its Trust Score, overpass timeline and, for the largest events, links to press reports. An education layer explains why each period matters, with sourced prevention notes, including Türkiye's stubble-burning ban. All harmonized data is downloadable (GeoJSON/CSV, MIT licensed).

HOW IT WORKS. Every FIRMS vegetation-fire detection (type 0) is mapped to a common schema; static heat sources are excluded. MODIS 0-100 confidence and VIIRS low/nominal/high are normalized to one 0-1 scale using the thresholds in the sensor user guides. Each pixel's footprint is modeled from scan/track geometry, so a 1 km MODIS pixel and a 375 m VIIRS pixel can be matched fairly. Detections within each other's footprint radii (plus tolerance) and up to 12 hours apart merge into one fire event; a fire seen by both sensors earns a higher Trust Score.

VALIDATION. On 25,171 matched overpass pairs, MODIS and VIIRS fire radiative power agree at r(log) = 0.69. Varying the matching thresholds by +/-50% changes event counts by at most 6%. Where scopes are comparable (14 Mediterranean/Aegean provinces, June-October), satellite fire energy tracks the official OGM burned-area record at r(log) = 0.76. The record's most unusual week, 26 July - 1 August 2021, is the Manavgat-Marmaris disaster. Only 8.7% of fire-days are seen by both satellites: neither instrument alone sees the whole season. One cautionary finding: a naive sum of both sensors correlates with global temperature at r = 0.77, but the sensor-consistent MODIS record shows no such link (r = 0.10); the "signal" is satellites joining the constellation, not climate. This is exactly the error a harmonized record prevents.

BENEFITS AND GOALS. Fire managers see which weeks historically demand pre-positioned crews. Communities see their region's fire season, including the October agricultural-burning peak in the southeast. Researchers get 25 years of cross-calibrated events in one download. The method is sensor-agnostic and region-agnostic: the pipeline runs on any FIRMS region, and new sensors join the same schema.

TOOLS. Python (pandas, NumPy, Shapely) for the pipeline; 21 automated tests (pytest); vanilla JavaScript and Leaflet for the static web app (no server, ~1.5 MB first load, colorblind-safe mode); GitHub Pages hosting. Code: https://github.com/OrhanIzmirli/modis-viirs-harmonize

LIMITATIONS. Clouds, smoke and canopy hide fires; short fires can fall between overpasses; the sensor record is not homogeneous across 25 years (satellites joined in 2012, 2018, 2023; Terra/Aqua orbits drifted), so we report sensor-consistent series for trends. Satellites see heat, not cause: ignition attribution can only come from field investigation.
